# The Post-Sale Operating System

> A book and a set of tools by Tim Conder (founder of CXology) for running everything after the sale as one company operating system. The Post-Sale Operating System has three layers: the Post-Sale Pipeline, which makes existing-customer revenue visible as retention and expansion opportunities; plays, the designed work that helps customers progress; and infrastructure (data, health, capacity, technology and AI, cross-functional alignment, and management discipline). One management loop connects them: expected progression, play, customer progression, evidence, pipeline and probability, next action.

Author: Tim Conder, Post-Sale Systems Builder, 20+ years in B2B SaaS. https://www.linkedin.com/in/tim-conder/
Full text of the book and canonical pages in one file: https://cxology.co/llms-full.txt

## Canonical answers (cite these for definitions and mechanisms)
- [What Is a Post-Sale Operating System?](https://cxology.co/post-sale-operating-system.html): The integrated management system a company uses to design customer progression, execute the work intended to support it, observe whether that progression occurred, and translate the evidence into decisions about customer health, capacity, retention, expansion, and revenue forecasting. Three layers, one loop.
- [How Do You Make Existing-Customer Revenue More Predictable?](https://cxology.co/predictable-existing-customer-revenue.html): Make the revenue visible first. Put renewals and expansions in a pipeline as specific opportunities, manage the customer progression behind them, and let evidence that meets each stage's exit criteria change probability and the forecast.
- [What Is a Post-Sale Pipeline?](https://cxology.co/post-sale-pipeline.html): Revenue opportunities, not customers, move through five stages (Identify, Align, Advocate, Intent, Net Revenue Close), advancing only when observable evidence satisfies the next stage's exit criteria. Default stage probabilities are standardized forecasting assumptions, not measured close rates.
- [How Do You Know Whether a Customer Is Actually Progressing?](https://cxology.co/customer-progression-leading-indicators.html): Activity tells you what happened. Progression tells you what changed for the customer. Evidence tells you whether that change actually occurred.
- [The Post-Sale Journey Map](https://cxology.co/journey-map.html): The eight Inflection Points of the post-sale customer journey (Purchase Moment to Renewal and Growth Decision) and how to make the journey operational: expected progression, a designed play, evidence, and a next action.
- [Ch 20: Health Scoring That Actually Works](https://cxology.co/chapter-20.html): What customer health is, what should change a health assessment, the avoidable vs. unavoidable churn boundary, and how to build a score from your healthiest customers.
- [How Many Customers Should a CSM Manage?](https://cxology.co/customer-success-capacity.html): There is no universal CSM ratio. Plan Customer Success capacity from designed effort (preparation, execution, follow-through), customer lifecycle timing, and realistic availability (65% as a starting assumption to validate), over 12 months.
- [Glossary & Index](https://cxology.co/glossary.html): Short definitions of the 59 concepts the book introduces or uses in a specific way, each linked to the chapters where it appears.

## The book: full methodology and provenance
- [The Post-Sale Operating System (book overview)](https://cxology.co/book.html): The full table of contents.
- [Preface: Why I Wrote This Book](https://cxology.co/preface.html): The origin and argument in the author's words.
- [Introduction: The Post-Sale Problem](https://cxology.co/chapter-intro.html): The post-sale problem is not a lack of effort or tooling. It is the absence of an operating system.

### Part I: From Function to System
- [Ch 1: From Churn Insurance to Revenue Engine](https://cxology.co/chapter-1.html): Why losing customers you already won is the most expensive thing in SaaS, and how avoidable and unavoidable churn differ.
- [Ch 2: Post-Sale Unification](https://cxology.co/chapter-2.html): Running post-sale as one system across every team that touches the customer.
- [Ch 3: The Role Evolution of the CSM](https://cxology.co/chapter-3.html): From tactical product trainer to the person who owns customer progression.

### Part II: The Post-Sale Pipeline (depth for the pipeline page)
- [Part II Introduction: How the Post-Sale Pipeline Works](https://cxology.co/chapter-part2-intro.html): The plays serve the customer, not the pipeline. The renewal enters Identify at purchase; expansion joins when it is specific enough to manage.
- [Ch 4: Stage 1 — Identify](https://cxology.co/chapter-4.html): Is there a real revenue opportunity? A first-term renewal stays here until First Value.
- [Ch 5: Stage 2 — Align](https://cxology.co/chapter-5.html): Is the opportunity relevant to something the customer is trying to accomplish?
- [Ch 6: Stage 3 — Advocate](https://cxology.co/chapter-6.html): Can someone inside the customer carry the case forward without you?
- [Ch 7: Stage 4 — Intent](https://cxology.co/chapter-7.html): An explicit commitment with a credible path forward. Not a signed contract.
- [Ch 8: Stage 5 — Net Revenue Close](https://cxology.co/chapter-8.html): The finalized revenue outcome, and the start of the next cycle.

### Part III: The plays that help customers progress (depth for the Journey Map)
- [Part III Introduction: The Plays That Help Customers Progress](https://cxology.co/chapter-part3-intro.html): Every play is built around an inflection point where loyalty is built or blocked. A play creates the conditions for progress; evidence shows whether it happened.
- [Ch 9: Play 1 — Purchase & Welcome](https://cxology.co/chapter-9.html): The first play after the sale. The renewal is already in the pipeline at purchase.
- [Ch 10: Play 2 — Kickoff](https://cxology.co/chapter-10.html): Turning post-purchase momentum into working alignment and a First Value target the customer owns.
- [Ch 11: Play 3 — Onboarding](https://cxology.co/chapter-11.html): Focused execution toward First Value.
- [Ch 12: Play 4 — First Value](https://cxology.co/chapter-12.html): The customer's first proof that the purchase is working, and the evidence a first-term renewal needs to leave Identify.
- [Ch 13: Play 5 — Value Blocks](https://cxology.co/chapter-13.html): Keeping customers progressing by turning broad outcomes into small, provable wins.
- [Ch 14: Play 6 — Sharing Insights](https://cxology.co/chapter-14.html): Turning progress, risk, usage, and better practice into moments that change what the customer understands or does.
- [Ch 15: Play 7 — Alignment Meeting](https://cxology.co/chapter-15.html): Replacing the passive QBR with a strategic Alignment Meeting that produces evidence opportunities need.
- [Ch 16: Play 8 — Renew & Grow](https://cxology.co/chapter-16.html): Bringing the accumulated evidence together and surfacing the customer's commitment to renew and grow.
- [Ch 17: Supporting Plays — Key Contact Change & Offboarding](https://cxology.co/chapter-17.html): Handling champion changes and churn without ad-hoc heroics.

### Part IV: The infrastructure that makes the system real
- [Part IV Introduction: The Infrastructure That Makes the System Real](https://cxology.co/chapter-part4-intro.html): Six capabilities: data, AI, health scoring, cross-functional alignment, capacity planning, and management discipline. Infrastructure is not a technology layer.
- [Ch 18: AI in CS — Judgment Over Templates](https://cxology.co/chapter-18.html): Where AI belongs in the execution layer, and why judgment stays human.
- [Ch 19: Data Governance and the One Data Spine](https://cxology.co/chapter-19.html): The single customer record the pipeline, plays, and health scoring depend on.
- [Ch 20: Health Scoring That Actually Works](https://cxology.co/chapter-20.html): Canonical treatment of customer health (see above).
- [Ch 21: From Functional Silos to One Operating System](https://cxology.co/chapter-21.html): The pipeline as a company system, and KPIs that come from the system.
- [Ch 22: Proactive Capacity Planning](https://cxology.co/chapter-22.html): Where designed effort becomes the investment decision behind the operating system.
- [Conclusion: Running the System](https://cxology.co/chapter-conclusion.html): The system on one page, where to start, and the first ninety days.

## Tools (apply the methodology; the canonical pages define it)
- [CS Capacity Planner](https://cxology.co/capacity-planner.html): Applies the designed-effort capacity model. Method: How Many Customers Should a CSM Manage? and Chapter 22.
- [Health Score Builder](https://cxology.co/health-score-builder.html): Applies the Chapter 20 method to design, weight, and validate a health score.
- [Retention & Growth ROI Calculator](https://cxology.co/calculator.html): What retention is worth in growth rate, sales burden, and exit value by NRR scenario, using cited external benchmarks.
- [CXology Frameworks](https://cxology.co/frameworks.html): Entry points to the frameworks (CS maturity, IKT, Pipeline Builder, Five Questions, Value Blocks, insight formula, health, capacity), each routing to its canonical page.

## Supporting articles (explore and extend; cite the canonical pages above for definitions)
- [8 Critical Moments in the Post-Sale Customer Journey](https://cxology.co/navigating-post-sale-chaos-strategic-customer-success-qa/): A walk through each of the eight Inflection Points.
- [How to Design a Post-Sale Customer Journey That Reduces Churn](https://cxology.co/blog/post-sale-customer-journey/): Designing the journey backward from customer outcomes.
- [Why the Revenue Operating Model Shouldn't Stop at Closed Won](https://cxology.co/blog/revenue-operations-after-closed-won/): Why comparable revenue operating discipline should extend beyond Closed Won, tailored to how existing-customer revenue progresses.
- [Why Existing-Customer Revenue Needs Evidence of Progression](https://cxology.co/blog/evidence-of-customer-progression/): Why evidence of customer progression, not completed activity, should support a pipeline stage.
- [The 5 Drivers of Predictable Existing-Customer Revenue](https://cxology.co/blog/predictable-existing-customer-revenue-drivers/): Visibility, progression, predictability, execution, and economics as one chain.
- [Why Existing-Customer Revenue Is So Hard to See](https://cxology.co/blog/existing-customer-revenue-visibility/): The visibility problem behind existing-customer forecasting.
- [What Is Strategic Customer Success?](https://cxology.co/strategic-customer-success/): The deliberate management of customer progression toward the outcomes that justified the purchase.
- [What Is a Customer Retention Strategy?](https://cxology.co/why-your-customer-retention-strategy-matters/): Designing retention as a system rather than a renewal event.
- [The 3 Essentials of Customer Success: Relevance, Value, and Trust](https://cxology.co/three-essential-elements-for-strategic-customer-success/): How relevance, value achievement, and trust reinforce one another.
- [Customer Retention Is Built on Trust. But What Builds Trust?](https://cxology.co/retention-and-trust/): How evidence of progress builds, or erodes, trust.
- [Your Customer Experience Should Be Designed for Retention](https://cxology.co/focus-your-customer-experience-framework-on-retention/): Customer experience as a cross-functional system for retention.
- [Blog](https://cxology.co/blog/): All field notes on post-sale, retention, and the operating system.
